commentary: Aquinas reads this opening chapter as Aristotle's attempt to mark off metaphysics from every other branch of knowledge by showing what is distinctive about its subject matter. Every science, he notes, goes searching for causes and starting points, but each of the particular sciences carves off some limited region of reality - a genus - and studies that alone, taking for granted that its subject exists and simply working out its properties. None of them asks the deeper question of what it means for something to be at all. Metaphysics alone takes being itself, considered simply as being, for its object, and so alone inquires into the causes and principles of everything without restriction. To make this vivid, Aquinas walks through the three theoretical sciences that Aristotle distinguishes according to their relation to matter and motion. Natural philosophy studies substances that involve both matter and change, since its objects cannot even be defined without reference to a movable subject. Mathematics studies things that are abstracted from sensible matter by the mind's own act of separation, even though such things do not actually exist apart from bodies. The highest of the three, which Aristotle calls theology and which Aquinas identifies with first philosophy, considers substance that is both immaterial and immovable in its very existence, not merely as conceived by abstraction. Because this third science treats the highest and most universal causes - causes on which the being of everything else depends - it deserves the name of first philosophy, and it is this science, Aquinas insists, that alone is equipped to study being as being.

Here Aquinas explains why Aristotle excludes accidental being from the concerns of metaphysics even though metaphysics studies being universally. He first lays out the different senses in which something can be said to be: being by accident, being as truth (a matter of how the mind joins or separates concepts), being according to the ten categories, and being as divided into potency and act. Having distinguished these, Aristotle sets aside the first two so that the science can concentrate on being under the categories, understood through potency and act. Aquinas's explanation of why accidental being escapes scientific treatment turns on the nature of science itself: genuine knowledge grasps what holds always or for the most part, tracing an effect back to a per se cause that reliably produces it. An accidental combination, such as a builder who happens also to be a physician and so happens to restore someone's health, involves no such regular connection; the joining of the two facts is a matter of coincidence rather than of one thing's nature producing another. Because such combinations have no determinate, per se cause, they cannot be foreseen, taught, or demonstrated, and so no art or science can be devoted to them. Aquinas connects this observation to the sophists, who trade precisely on confusing what belongs to a subject accidentally with what belongs to it essentially, generating deceptive arguments from that ambiguity. He also notes, importantly, that acknowledging accidental being does not commit one to denying necessity altogether in the world; it simply recognizes that alongside what happens always or usually, there remains a residue of things that merely happen to coincide, and these fall outside the reach of demonstrative knowledge.

In this chapter Aquinas presents Aristotle as answering a determinist who would deny that anything happens by chance at all, on the ground that every event follows of necessity from some prior cause, which in turn follows from an earlier cause, and so on back to causes already present or past - and what is already present or past cannot fail to have its effect. Aristotle's reply, as Aquinas unpacks it, is that this reasoning proves too much: if it were sound, absolutely everything that will ever happen would already be necessary now, which plainly conflicts with the evident fact that many things could go one way or another. The flaw lies in assuming that every causal chain must be unbroken and per se; in reality such chains regularly terminate in a cause that produces its effect only accidentally, not by its own proper power, and at that point the chain of necessity simply stops, leaving room for the event to have gone otherwise. Aquinas takes the occasion to relate this to broader questions about fate and divine providence, a topic he treats with some care. He explains that lower, particular causes can fail or be impeded by contrary circumstances, which is precisely why their effects are only usual rather than strictly necessary, and why free rational choice is not bound by the sweep of the heavenly bodies acting on bodily nature. Yet none of this contingency escapes the ordering of divine providence, which, precisely because it operates on an entirely higher level than any particular cause, can hold all things - including contingent and accidental happenings - within a single order without thereby forcing them to happen of necessity.

Having dismissed accidental being, Aquinas explains that Aristotle now turns to a second sense of being that likewise falls outside the proper scope of metaphysics: being as truth, and its opposite, non-being as falsity. His central claim, as Aquinas draws it out, is that truth and falsity are not features of things in the world taken by themselves, but belong strictly to the operation of the intellect. A thing simply is or is not what it is; it becomes true or false only in relation to a mind that either correctly or incorrectly represents it. More precisely, truth and falsity arise only where the intellect composes or divides - that is, where it affirms that some subject and predicate belong together or denies that they do. When the mind joins what is in fact united in reality, or separates what is in fact distinct, its judgment is true; when it does the reverse, the judgment is false. Aquinas stresses that this composing and dividing must be understood as an instantaneous act of the intellect grasping a single unified content, not a temporal succession of separate thoughts. He also notes that with regard to simple, uncomposed apprehension of what a thing is, there is no truth or falsity at all, since error only enters once the mind ventures to affirm or deny something of a subject. Because this sense of being tracks something added by the mind's own activity rather than the constitution of things themselves, it, like accidental being, must be set aside from the inquiry into being as being, clearing the ground for Aristotle to take up the causes and principles of substance properly speaking.
